items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: And that rhythm section, he had Walt Page, Jo Jones, because that was all the American rhythm section, and himself, Freddie Green.

ctx.x: A question I wanted to ask you is, you know Basie has been quoted as saying that his band was developed from the rhythm section, and then up through the tenor sax positions, and then to the rest of the band.

Yeah he loved tenors. You see in those days, you only had one tenor player, featured tenor player, but he always had two so he started out with Herschel and Lester. So he had two of the world’s greatest and wasn’t nobody — he had to make it. So when they went to New York they just chopped everybody down. And that rhythm section, he had Walt Page, Jo Jones, because that was all the American rhythm section, and himself, Freddie Green. That was quite a band.

I wanted to ask you about that particular sound. There were different sounds, they say a different feel to the music that there was in the southwest than on the west coast or in the New York scene. Could you describe for us how you felt the sound of the Basie band was different? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

items.title: 68097_Freddie Green oral history interview
items.q: Yeah. He's permanent on clarinet, you know -- after Herschel left.

ctx.x: Yeah. Buddy's there all that time.
Yeah. He's permanent on clarinet, you know -- after Herschel left.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, what I'd like to know, Stan, is in '46 when the rhythm section goes back to the original rhythm section -- you know -- let's not jump to '50 yet. I mean, in those four years are there all that many changes -- after the war is finished -- after it's no longer a question of people being drafted -- are there still all those changes occuring all the time in those four years?
